title: The difficult person
hookLine: begin with someone mildly difficult, never the hardest
last: MAJJHATTA — THEY HAVE A WHOLE LIFE.

lines: NOT THE ONE WHO HURT YOU.
cards: The coworker who replies all. The relative who comments on your plate at holidays. The neighbor with the leaf blower at seven in the morning.
A title like today's can call up faces fast. And further down the list, for some people, there's someone who really hurt them. Today is not about that person.
The old guidance is gentle and very practical: begin with someone mildly difficult, never the hardest. You don't learn to lift by starting with the heaviest thing in the gym.

teach.h: GO BACK TO AN EASIER PERSON.
teach.b: In the Visuddhimagga, after yourself, a benefactor, a friend and a neutral person, comes the hostile person. Buddhaghosa is honest: resentment will come up. So he gives a whole toolbox.
One: go back to an easier person, warm up, and return. Two: remember what the Buddha taught about anger; the manual quotes his sayings on it.
The Dhammapada has one in its first chapter, in Max Müller's 1881 translation: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love." And it calls that an old rule.
Three: look for one good quality in the difficult person. Maybe their words are harsh, but they work hard. Maybe they're prickly, but they're good to their dog.
If you truly can't find one, the manual says, feel compassion: this person is headed for trouble of their own making. Four, the vivid one: anger hurts you first.
Buddhaghosa compares getting angry at someone to picking up a burning coal with your bare hand to throw at them. You get burned before they do. None of this says what the person did was fine.
Metta isn't approval. It isn't staying in a harmful situation. It's a wish that they be well, which, honestly, often means a wish that they become less difficult.
You're not asked for great warmth toward the leaf-blower neighbor, just a sincere drop: a little, honestly. One honest wish, even a small one, does more than a big pretend one.

how: Modern Buddhist teachers often advise beginning metta for a difficult person with someone only mildly difficult, and never forcing the practice toward someone who caused serious harm.

games.q: the manual's toolbox — tap the pairs.

s: metta for a difficult person means approving of what they did
metta is a wish for their good. it isn't approval, and it isn't staying in harm.
the guidance says to start with the person who hurt you most
begin with someone mildly difficult, never the hardest.
Buddhaghosa compares anger to picking up a burning coal
you're burned before the other person is.

games.q: you're trying metta for a difficult coworker and can't find anything good about them. what does the manual suggest?
o: feel compassion: they're heading for trouble of their own making.
games.why: if no good quality can be found, Buddhaghosa suggests compassion for the suffering their conduct will bring them.

practice: Warm up with the phrases for yourself first: may I be safe, happy, healthy, at ease.

Then bring to mind someone who just irritates you, not the hardest, notice what the jaw and shoulders do, and for one breath offer them one phrase: may you be at ease. If it's too much, go back to yourself, and try again.

wordCard.voice: Vera. Enmity, hatred: the fifth step of metta, someone mildly hard, met with a small, honest wish.

orig.note: Pali: enmity, hatred; the Dhammapada's first chapter says vera is not ended by vera.

carryVoice: Your line: a little, honestly. Metta isn't approval; it's a wish for their good. That's day one hundred and two.
